071.subtitle: A queen in her own right, and bells at the waist

commentary.meaning: Eight names, and every one of them begins with the same letter. The verse opens at the top of the political order and immediately does something unexpected with it: the king of kings is not what she is called but what worships her, and the name she does take, rājñī, is the feminine of the word for a king rather than any of the words for a king's wife. Sovereignty settled in one name, the verse spends everything else on pleasure. She is delightful; her eyes have the long cool shape of the blue lotus; she colours the mind the way a dye takes to cloth; she is a lovely woman; she is the savour that makes anything worth having at all. Then the last name puts a sound in the room — the small bells strung along the belt at her waist, ringing because she has just moved. The arrangement is deliberate. Power is stated once and dropped. What fills the verse is the quality of being enjoyable, and it ends not on a throne but on a waist and a noise.
commentary.history:
This verse opens one of the alliterative runs that give the middle of the stotra its shape. Sixteen consecutive names, all of this verse and all of the next, begin with r; then verses 73 and 74 turn to k, verse 75 to v, verse 76 to a solid block of kṣ, verse 77 back to v. The thousand names are not arranged alphabetically, and there is no acrostic to decode, but these runs are unmistakable once you notice them, and they are the sort of thing a text composed for memorisation and for recitation aloud does on purpose. A hundred names that share an initial sound are a hundred names that can be checked against each other while chanting.

The recension this site follows marks a section boundary immediately before this verse. It divides the thousand names into ten hundreds and labels each hundred with a digit of the sun — tāpinī for names 1 to 100, then dhūmrikā, marīcī, and jvālinī for 301 to 400, which is where this verse sits, running on through rucī, suṣumṇā, bhogadā, viśvā, bodhinī and dhāriṇī. Those are the second through the eleventh of the twelve solar kalās named in the Nārada Purāṇa and the Mahānirvāṇa Tantra. Jvālinī means the flaming one, and it is worth registering that a hundred named for a tongue of fire opens with sixteen names on r, the letter tantric lore treats as fire; Monier-Williams records vahni as a mystical name of r.

Rājarāja is a title rather than a person, and the dictionary gives three things it can mean: a supreme sovereign or emperor, Kubera the lord of wealth, and the moon. Commentators generally take Kubera here, which sharpens the name considerably: the richest being in the cosmos, the treasurer of the gods, is on the wrong side of the transaction. Note also the grammar. Arcitā is a past passive participle, so the name is not an action of hers; it describes what is done to her. This is the first of an unusually dense run of such names. Within the next fourteen verses she is worshipped by the guardians of holy ground, by ascetics who have burnt everything else away, by the god of desire in person, and by a rite performed behind closed doors — the whole range of who worships, from the wealthiest to the most renounced, with desire itself on the list.

Rājñī is a small grammatical event. It is the feminine formed directly from rājan, king, by the suffix that makes agent-nouns feminine, and Sanskrit had perfectly good alternatives — mahiṣī, the chief queen, or a compound in patnī, wife. The word chosen is the one for a woman who rules, and the Vedic hymn in which the goddess speaks in her own voice uses its exact synonym: ahaṃ rāṣṭrī, I am sovereignty. Read beside kāmeśvaraprāṇanāḍī fourteen verses further on, where she is the artery carrying her consort's life, the picture is consistent. She is not queen because she is married to a king.

Two of the pleasure-names repay a look at their roots. Rañjanī comes from √rañj, which means both to be dyed or reddened and to be delighted or charmed; the same root gives rāga, which is colour and passion and, later, a musical mode, and rakta, which is red and also in love. In Sanskrit the mind that is gladdened and the cloth that is dyed undergo the same verb, and in a hymn whose colour has been red since its first verse the pun is not accidental. Rasyā rests on rasa — sap, juice, taste, the essence of a thing, and in poetics the flavour a work leaves in the audience. Three rasa-names fall inside these fifteen verses: rasyā here, the ocean of the flavour of compassion two verses on, and brimful of the erotic flavour eleven verses after that.

Rājīva looks like another word built on rājan and is not. The dictionary's first sense for it is streaked or striped, and the same form names a striped deer, a crane, an elephant and a species of fish before it settles, in the neuter, on the blue lotus. The likeness to rājan is purely a matter of sound, which in a verse organised entirely by sound is the point. It is also worth knowing that rājīvalocana, lotus-eyed, is one of the standard epithets of Viṣṇu and of Rāma. Handing it to her, one name before handing her Lakṣmī's name outright in the next verse, is the same quiet annexation performed twice.

The last name is the only sound in the verse. Mekhalā is a girdle or belt, and the dictionary's principal entry is not ornamental at all: it is the ritual cord tied round an initiate at his investiture, of muñja grass for a brahmin. The same word covers a woman's jewelled belt and an ascetic's waist-cord. Raṇat is a present participle, ringing now, not rung; and this is the second time the hymn has described this belt. At name 38 it was ratnakiṅkiṇikāramyaraśanādāmabhūṣitā, adorned with a girdle-string lovely with jewelled bells — seen and not heard. Two hundred and seventy-four names later the same object is given back to us as noise.
commentary.practice:
The metre is anuṣṭubh throughout, eight syllables to the quarter, and the break falls cleanly between names: rājarājārcitā rājñī, then ramyā rājīvalocanā. The second line is four names, of which the last takes a full eight syllables to itself, so the rhythm of the verse is short-short-short-long in each half.

The first thing to fix is the r itself, because there are sixteen of them and nothing else in the verse will survive getting it wrong. The Sanskrit r is a single quick tap of the tongue-tip just behind the upper teeth. It is not the English r, which is made with the tongue bunched and the tip curled back and touching nothing, and a line of English r's turns this verse into mud. Say ra-ra-ra slowly with a visible tap, then run rājarājārcitā at half speed and listen for four distinct contacts.

Rājñī contains the conjunct jñ, written राज्ञी: the letter ja joined to the palatal nasal ña, with the long ī sign after. This is the single most regionally variable cluster in Sanskrit. Northern reciters generally say something like gy, Marathi speakers dnya, southern reciters an analytic j followed by ñ. The grammarians describe two palatal sounds in sequence, which is what the letters actually say, and that is the safest thing to teach your mouth; whichever you adopt, use the same one in kṛtajñā eleven verses later so that your text stays consistent with itself.

The verse is also a complete drill in nasal assimilation. Rañjanī has the palatal ñ before the palatal j; kiṅkiṇi has the guttural ṅ before k and then the retroflex ṇ; ramaṇī and raṇat have the retroflex ṇ. The rule underneath all of this is that a Sanskrit nasal takes the position of the stop that follows it, so the tongue never travels between the nasal and the consonant after it. In रञ्जनी it is already at the palate for the ñ and stays there for the ja; in किङ्किणि it is already at the soft palate for the ṅ and stays there for the ka. If you find yourself moving, you are inserting a sound that is not there.

Rasyā needs a clean dental s before the y — not the palatal ś, and not the English sh, which is where an unwary tongue drifts when a y follows. And keep the vowel lengths honest: the long ā of rāja- and rājīva- against the uniformly short a of ramaṇī and rañjanī. Ramyā is short then long; ramā in the very next verse is short then long as well, and rāmā, four names after that, is long-long.

One practical note for anyone using the nāmāvalī. The dative forms in this recension run rājarājārcitāyai, ramyāyai, rañjanyai, ramaṇyai, rasyāyai — and, for the queen, rājñai, where the ī-stem paradigm would lead you to expect rājñyai. Printed nāmāvalīs are not unanimous about forms like this, and it is worth checking against whichever book you actually use for archanā.

As for what to hold while chanting: the verse ends on a sound made by a moving body, which is also what chanting is. The last name comes closer than anything else in the stotra to describing what you are doing while you say it.

072.subtitle: Fortune, the full moon, and a goddess greedy for her lover

commentary.meaning: The run on r continues for eight more names, and the verse covers an extraordinary distance without ever changing its opening letter. It begins by giving her Lakṣmī's own name, Ramā, so that prosperity is not something she grants but something she is. Her face is the moon of the full-moon night. Then two names of Rati, the wife of the god of love: she has Rati's form, and Rati's pleasure is dear to her. Halfway through, the register breaks. She makes a guard around those who come to her, and she kills the beings one needs guarding from. Then it breaks back: she is simply a beautiful woman, and the last name says, in the plainest and least decorous vocabulary the hymn has yet used, that she is greedy for her lover. Fortune, beauty, eros, violence, eros again. A hymn that wanted these to be separate departments of the divine would have given them separate verses.
commentary.history:
Ramā is Lakṣmī's name, and it is being used here without apology or explanation. Śākta hymns absorb rather than argue: the goddess who is Lalitā is also the goddess of good fortune, and a few hundred names later the same text will hand her Sarasvatī's functions too. What makes the annexation graceful is that ramā earns its place in the alliteration honestly, since it comes from √ram, to delight or take pleasure, the same root as ramyā and ramaṇī in the verse before and rāmā and ramaṇa in this one. Six of the sixteen names in this pair of verses are built on that one root. The Śrī Sūkta, the old Vedic appendix-hymn that is still the standard liturgy for Lakṣmī, describes her as moon-like and golden, which is exactly the pairing this verse makes in its first two names.

Rākā is not a general word for fullness. The dictionary's first sense is a goddess: the deity who presides over the actual day of the full moon, with her sister Anumati presiding over the day before it. She is invoked by name in the Ṛgveda. So rākendu is not simply the full moon, it is the moon of the night that has a goddess of its own, and the compound quietly puts one goddess inside another. It is also a correction of scale. Verse 5 of this stotra gave her the moon of the eighth night, exactly half a disc, for a forehead. Sixty-seven verses later the disc has filled.

The two Rati names are grounded in the narrative this hymn belongs to, and the connection is specific. In the Lalitopākhyāna, the section of the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa that carries this stotra, Bhaṇḍāsura — the demon Lalitā takes form in order to destroy — is made from the ashes of Kāma after Śiva burns him. When Bhaṇḍa has been destroyed, the gods bring Rati, widowed by the same fire that eventually produced the demon, and ask Lalitā to give her husband back. She does. The chain is worth holding in mind: the god of love is burnt, his ashes become the enemy, the goddess destroys the enemy, and then she restores the god of love to the wife who lost him. Ratipriyā, the pleasure of love is dear to her, is not a decorative compliment in that story. It is what she actually did.

Rakṣākarī and rākṣasaghnī are the same root turned in opposite directions, and this is visible in the words rather than merely available to a commentator. Rakṣā is protection, from √rakṣ, to guard. Rakṣas, from which rākṣasa is formed, is glossed by the dictionary as anything to be guarded against or warded off — harm, injury — before it means a demon at all. So the pair says: she is the guarding, and she is the destruction of the thing one guards against. Sanskrit gets to make that argument in two words because the vocabulary of protection and the vocabulary of monsters share an origin, and the purāṇic literature has an old story that turns on exactly this, deriving one class of beings from the cry rakṣāma, let us guard, at the moment of their creation.

Ramaṇalampaṭā is the name that stops readers. Lampaṭa is not a polite word. The dictionary gives covetous, greedy, lustful, addicted to, and as a noun a libertine or a lecher; it is the word for someone whose appetite is a character flaw. Applied to the supreme goddess, in the accusative of her own consort, it is deliberate. The Śrīvidyā reading is that the eagerness is metaphysical rather than merely amorous: Śiva without Śakti cannot so much as stir, and Śakti's inclination toward him is the tension that holds the manifest world in being, so a word for insatiability is exactly right and any milder word would be false. But it is worth noticing the plain fact first, before the metaphysics arrives. This hymn is at ease with a language for the divine that a Vaiṣṇava thousand-name hymn would not use, and it is at ease with it in the same verse in which the goddess kills demons.
commentary.practice:
The verse's difficulty is not in any single hard cluster but in vowel length, and it is unforgiving. Ramā, the second name, is short-long. Rāmā, seven names later, is long-long. They are different words: ramā is Lakṣmī, rāmā is simply a beautiful woman. Between them sit rāka- with a long ā, rati- with a short a twice, rakṣā- with a short a and a long ā, and rākṣasa- with a long ā and a short a. Take the eight names slowly in a row and mark each vowel long or short before you chant the verse at speed; nothing else in these fifteen verses depends so completely on getting quantity right.

Rākṣasaghnī has the hardest consonant sequence. The kṣ is k followed by the retroflex ṣ — never an English x — and then ghn is an aspirated voiced g running straight into n, which English never asks a mouth to do. Break it as rāk-ṣa-sagh-nī and let the breath of the gh carry into the n rather than stopping between them. The -ghnī ending is a real feminine agent noun from √han, to strike or kill, with the h and n changing places in the way that root always does when it forms compounds; you have already seen the same root in the meditation verses and will see it again in tamopahā at name 361.

Rākenduvadanā hides a sandhi that the Devanagari shows plainly once you look for it. Rākā plus indu, moon, gives rākendu: a final ā and an initial i have merged into a single e, written with the stroke े over क. This is the same fusion that produced manorūpekṣu in the third verse. If you cannot hear a word-boundary there it is because there is not one any more.

Two smaller points of articulation. In lampaṭā the m assimilates to the labial p that follows — the lips are already closed for the nasal and stay closed — and the ṭa is retroflex, made with the tongue-tip curled back, not the dental t. In ratirūpā and ratipriyā the two names are rhythmically identical apart from the pr cluster, so they should sound like a matched pair; reciters often run them together, and the metre allows it.

The caesura falls after rākenduvadanā in the first line and after rākṣasaghnī in the second, which means the line break lands exactly on the verse's change of subject, from beauty to violence and back. If you take a light breath at those two points you are also marking the argument.

For contemplation: this is a good verse on which to stop resisting the hymn's range. Nothing in it is arranged to make the goddess consistent by the standards of ordinary decorum. Fortune, the full moon, erotic pleasure, armed protection, killing, and unembarrassed desire are given eight names and one letter, and the text plainly considers them one subject. Chanting it as though the middle two names belonged to a different deity from the last one is a way of not hearing it.

073.subtitle: Desire drawn as a diagram, and a bulb under the soil

commentary.meaning: Six names, and the verse moves from the most abstract thing it can say to the most concrete and then back out again. It opens with desirability as such: she is kāmyā, the thing wanted, which is to say that every particular want is aimed at her whether or not it knows so. The second name gives that abstraction a shape — the kāmakalā, a small figure of points and letters in which desire and the form desire takes are drawn together, and which the tradition regards as her body. Then, without transition, a flower: the heavy orange globe of the kadamba, which is what she likes to be given. Then auspiciousness, the word one says over a beginning. And then two names of scale, both of them borrowed from the world rather than from philosophy. She is the bulb underground out of which the world comes up like a shoot, and she is a sea, and what the sea is made of is pity. A verse that started with a metaphysical claim ends by measuring compassion in cubic miles.
commentary.history:
Kāmyā is a gerundive: the one to be desired, the desirable. Read on its own it is a compliment. Read against the passage in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka in which Yājñavalkya explains to his wife why anything at all is dear to anyone, it becomes an argument. Nothing, he says, is dear for its own sake; husband, wife, children, wealth and even brahminhood are dear for the sake of the self. If that is true, then whatever is genuinely desirable in anything is the self showing through it, and a name that says she is the desirable is a name that identifies her with the self. This is how Śākta texts characteristically do Vedānta — not by argument but by making the conclusion a name and moving on.

Kāmakalārūpā is the first frankly esoteric name in this stretch of the hymn, and it needs care, because the texts that describe the kāmakalā treat it as restricted knowledge and describe it in code. The word itself is transparent: kāma, desire, and kalā, a part, a portion, a digit of the moon, an art. What it denotes is a figure — three points arranged as a triangle, with a fourth element below — which is at once a diagram, a syllable, and a body. The classical treatment is the Kāmakalāvilāsa of Puṇyānanda, a short and difficult work with a commentary by Naṭanānandanātha, and its account is worked out in terms of the bindu, the point in which speech and light are held before either has separated out. The clearest thing a beginner can actually look at is Saundaryalaharī 19, which spells the visual arrangement out: the face as the point above, the two breasts below it, and below those the half-form of Hara. Note that Monier-Williams, whose 1899 dictionary is otherwise so good on this vocabulary, has only "a name of Rati" for kāmakalā. There are parts of this tradition that the lexicon simply does not reach, and this is one of them.

The kadamba is Neolamarckia cadamba, a large tree of the Indian plains whose flowers are borne in dense orange globes and open at the start of the rains. Its association with Śrīvidyā is not casual. Śaṅkara's description of her island in the sea of nectar plants it with a grove of nīpa, which is the kadamba under another name, so the tree she likes flowers where she lives. In the south the same connection is fixed to the ground: Madurai, the great temple city of the goddess Mīnākṣī, has been called the kadamba forest, and the tree is the temple's own. The attendant goddess Śyāmalā is likewise placed in a kadamba wood. When a name says a flower is dear to her it is reporting an offering that is actually made.

Jagatīkandā takes a different picture of origin from the one the upaniṣads made famous. A kanda is a bulb or tuber — the dictionary lists garlic and elephant-foot yam among its senses — and the point of a bulb is that it is underground, unimpressive, and not the plant you can see. The world is the shoot; she is the swelling below the soil that the shoot comes out of. Set this against the Muṇḍaka's images for the same relation, the spider spinning out its thread and hair growing on a living body, and the family resemblance is clear: what is wanted in all of them is a source that stays in continuous material relation with what comes from it, rather than a maker standing outside its product. The word also has a technical life in yoga, where kanda names the bulb at the base of the trunk from which the channels of the subtle body are said to spring — a sense that will matter nine verses later when she is called the artery that carries Kāmeśvara's breath.

The last name is a rasa name, the second of three in these fifteen verses. Karuṇa is not simply pity; it is one of the eight flavours catalogued by Sanskrit dramatic theory, the flavour of grief and compassion, and putting rasa into the compound rather than saying karuṇāsāgarā means the name is using the technical vocabulary on purpose. What she is an ocean of is not an emotion she feels but a savour that can be tasted — the same category as the delight of name 311 in the verse before and the erotic flavour of name 376 eleven verses ahead. The three together are a small argument about what the goddess is: not a being who has states, but the taste of the states themselves.
commentary.practice:
Six names, all beginning with k except the fifth, and the caesura is clean: kāmyā kāmakalārūpā, then kadambakusumapriyā; kalyāṇī jagatīkandā, then karuṇārasasāgarā. The two long names each fill a half-line exactly.

The consonant to watch is the unaspirated k. Sanskrit distinguishes k from kh absolutely, and English speakers aspirate every initial k without noticing — the puff of air that follows the k in "kite" would make kāmyā into khāmyā, which is a different word. Hold the back of your hand in front of your mouth and say kāmyā, kadamba, kalyāṇī, karuṇā; if you feel breath, the k is wrong. This verse gives you five chances in a row to fix it.

Kāmyā opens with the cluster my, labial nasal into palatal glide, which wants to become miya if you let it. Keep it as one beat: kām-yā, two syllables, not three. Kalyāṇī has the parallel cluster ly and then a retroflex ṇ; the tongue-tip is at the teeth for the l, at the palate for the y, and curled right back for the ṇ, three distinct positions in four syllables. Say it slowly enough to feel all three.

Karuṇārasasāgarā is the rhythmic problem of the verse. It is eight syllables of which six are short a and two are long ā, and the temptation is to even them out into a jog. The long syllables are the fourth and the seventh — ka-ru-ṇā-ra-sa-sā-ga-rā — with a final long ā as well, and the retroflex ṇ sits just before the first of them. Chant it four times on its own, exaggerating the length of nā and sā, before you put it back in the line.

Two sandhis are worth reconstructing. Kāmakalā plus rūpā simply juxtaposes two words with no change, but jagatī plus kanda produces jagatīkandā with the long ī of the first member preserved — a reminder that ī-stems in compounds do not shorten the way one might expect from the Devanagari. And the third name is a straightforward chain, kadamba-kusuma-priyā, three words in a row with no fusion at all, which makes it a good one to break apart and reassemble while reading the script.

On what to hold in mind: this verse asks for two quite different kinds of attention within eight seconds. The second name points at something the tradition does not explain in public, and the honest posture towards it while chanting is neither to pretend to understand nor to skip past it, but to say it accurately and leave it standing. The fifth and sixth names ask for the opposite — they are entirely concrete, a bulb and a body of water, and they reward being pictured. The kadamba between them is the hinge: an actual flower, of a real tree, which someone somewhere is putting in front of her image at the moment you are chanting.

074.subtitle: Wine made from the flower of the previous verse

commentary.meaning: Seven names, and the alliteration changes gear halfway through: four on k, then three on v, with the join falling exactly at the line break. The k names give her the arts, a soft indistinct voice, the plain word for a woman who is loved, and a taste for kādambarī, the liquor pressed from kadamba flowers — the same tree whose blossoms the verse before said were her favourite offering. The v names give a boon, a pair of beautiful eyes, and then the closing image, which is startling in a hymn to the supreme: she is unsteady, swaying, not in command of herself, because the vāruṇī liquor has gone to her head. Put the first and last names of the verse side by side and the shape of it appears. She is mistress of every skill there is, and she is drunk. Between them stands varadā, granter of boons: the one name in the verse about what she does for anybody else, set among six about what she is like.
commentary.history:
Kalā is one of the most productive words in this vocabulary and the name kalāvatī cashes in on all of it at once. The dictionary's first sense is a small part of anything, especially a sixteenth part; from that come the digit of the moon, a division of time, and the fine arts, of which the tradition counts sixty-four. A possessive in -vat on such a stem means she has them all, and the hymn has already said so more explicitly at name 236, catuḥṣaṣṭikalāmayī, made of the sixty-four arts. The lunar sense is not idle either: eleven verses further on she will be called the sixteen eternal goddesses, and the sixteenth digit of the moon is the one that does not wane.

Kalālāpā looks like the same word again and is not. Kala, with a short final a, is a separate entry: indistinct, inarticulate, and then low, soft, melodious — the dictionary's example of it is a voice thick with tears. Ālāpa is speaking, conversation, and also the twittering of birds; in music it is still the word for the unmetred exploration that opens a performance. So the name does not say her speech is artful. It says it is soft and not quite articulate, which in Sanskrit poetics is a compliment of a specific kind, and it sits three names before a verse about wine and four verses before the hymn takes up the stages of speech in earnest.

Kādambarī is the richest word in the verse. The dictionary's entry for kādambara gives a spirit distilled from the flowers of the kadamba tree, and then something better: the rainwater that collects in hollows of the same tree when the flowers are at their peak, which is supposed to be sweetened by them. Either way the drink comes out of the tree named one verse earlier, and the two verses read as a single gesture — she likes the flower, and she likes what the flower is turned into. The word carries two more things. Kādambarī is a name of Sarasvatī, and it is the title of Bāṇa's seventh-century romance, the most famous prose narrative in Sanskrit, named after its heroine. A hymn that has just called her soft-spoken now gives her a word that means liquor, the goddess of speech, and a novel.

Vāruṇī is likewise a person before it is a substance. The dictionary makes her Varuṇa's female energy, produced at the churning of the ocean and presiding over spirituous liquor — so this is the second time in four verses that a goddess has been folded into a compound, after rākā the goddess of the full-moon night. And the picture of a goddess who has been drinking is much older than any tantra: in the Devī Māhātmya, Caṇḍikā drinks again and again in the middle of the battle with Mahiṣa, laughs, and goes back to killing him with her eyes red.

What the tradition does with the wine is the interesting question, and it is one on which Śrīvidyā has never been of one mind. In kaula lineages madya is one of the five substances of the ritual and is actually offered. In the samaya or right-hand form dominant in the south, everything of that kind is read internally: the liquor is the nectar that drips from the moon at the crown of the head when the practitioner's attention reaches it, so the intoxication described here is a physiological event in the subtle body and not a beverage. Both sides quote names like this one. What the name itself will not let either side avoid is vihvalā, which means overcome, unsteady, at a loss — a word for someone who is not in control. The hymn is willing to say that of her, in the same verse in which it calls her the giver of boons. This is not the only time; at name 577 she is mādhvīpānālasā and mattā, languid from drinking honey-wine, and simply drunk.
commentary.practice:
The verse is eight and eight, with the names falling neatly: kalāvatī kalālāpā, then kāntā kādambarīpriyā; varadā vāmanayanā, then vāruṇīmadavihvalā. The change of initial consonant happens across the line break, so the two halves sound like two different verses joined.

The first pair is a vowel-quantity trap laid deliberately. Kalāvatī is ka-lā-va-tī, short then long. Kalālāpā is ka-lā-lā-pā, with three long syllables running. And the underlying words differ: kalā with a long final ā in the first name, kala with a short a in the second. Say the two names slowly one after the other and make the difference audible; if they sound the same you have flattened a distinction the poet is using.

The hardest single sound in these fifteen verses is the hv of vihvalā, written विह्वला with ह् joined to व. It is a voiced h running straight into a v with no vowel between them, and English never asks for this. Do not insert a vowel — vi-ha-va-lā is wrong — and do not drop the h. Start the h with the voice already on, as in the middle of "ahead", and let the lips come to the v while it is still sounding. Three or four slow repetitions of vi-hva-lā will do more than reading about it.

The v itself needs attention throughout the second line, and again in the next three verses, which are full of it. Sanskrit v is made with the lower lip approaching the upper teeth without the full buzzing contact of an English v; after another consonant, as in svāhā or in the sv of the next verse but two, it is closer to an English w. What it is never is a b. Reciters from some regions merge the two, and vāruṇī becoming bāruṇī changes the word.

Kāntā has a dental nt: tongue-tip at the back of the upper teeth for both, not curled back. Kādambarī has a long ā, then short a, then short a — kā-dam-ba-rī — and the temptation is to lengthen the dam because of the m. Vāruṇī has a retroflex ṇ, tongue curled well back. And varadā, sitting between all these long syllables, is three short vowels and a long: va-ra-dā, light and quick.

The last name is a compound of three words and worth taking apart in the script before chanting it: वारुणी + मद + विह्वला, the liquor, the intoxication, and the state of being overcome, with no sandhi anywhere to disguise the joins. Reciters usually take the breath after vāmanayanā, which puts the whole of that eight-syllable name in one arc.

For contemplation: hold the first name and the last together rather than letting the verse drift. Complete mastery of every art, and a body that is not steady. The tradition has spent a great deal of ink deciding what the wine is, and the chanting does not require that question to be settled — but it does require that the name be said without flinching, because a hymn that describes the supreme as swaying is telling you something about what it thinks the supreme is like.

075.subtitle: Greater than everything, and living in a particular range of hills

commentary.meaning: Seven names on v, and the verse keeps changing the scale on which it is speaking. It opens as large as language allows — set her beside the universe and there is something left over — and follows that with a claim about how she is known: through the Veda. Then, without warning, an address. She lives in the Vindhya hills. The second line goes back up: she is the one who arranges how things will fall out, the Vedas are born from her, she is the power by which Viṣṇu holds the world together as an appearance, and she is play itself. The two Veda names are the hinge. If she is knowable through the Veda and the Veda is born from her, then the only road to her is one she built, and the verse says both things four names apart without appearing to notice a difficulty. Between them it puts her on a specific mountain, which is the sort of thing this hymn does when it is at its most confident.
commentary.history:
Viśvādhikā is a comparative built with an ablative: greater than the universe, exceeding it. The Puruṣa Sūkta had made the same claim by arithmetic — all beings are one quarter of him and three quarters stand immortal beyond — and the point of such formulations is to block the inference that if the divine is everything then it is exhausted by everything. The name is doing philosophical work in four syllables, and the work is the ordinary work of Vedānta, which is a good reminder that this hymn's tantric material sits inside a Vedāntic frame rather than beside it.

The two Veda names are best read as a pair even though three names separate them. Vedavedyā, to be known by means of the Vedas, is what a defender of the tradition's orthodoxy would want to say; the Gītā says it of Kṛṣṇa in almost the same words. Vedajananī, mother of the Vedas, reverses the dependency. Śrīvidyā spent much of its literary energy on exactly this manoeuvre, arguing that its mantra and its goddess were not extraneous to the Veda but its source and its secret meaning, and that a brahmin could therefore practise both without contradiction. The two names are that argument in miniature, and their placement on either side of a mountain address is a fair picture of how the text works: doctrine, geography, doctrine.

The Vindhyas are not a symbol. They are the range that runs east to west across the middle of the subcontinent and that Sanskrit geography treats as the boundary between the north and the south — a frontier, in older literature a place of forests and of peoples outside brahminical order. The goddess of that range, Vindhyavāsinī, has a temple at Vindhyachal near Mirzapur on the Ganges which is still one of the busiest goddess shrines in north India, and she was a major independent deity long before this hymn. The Devī Māhātmya records her at the moment of absorption: in the last chapter the goddess predicts her own future arrivals and says she will be born in the cowherd Nanda's house from Yaśodā's womb and, dwelling on the Vindhya mountain, destroy the demons. That verse is doing two things at once — attaching the Vindhya goddess to the Kṛṣṇa story, in which the infant girl exchanged for Kṛṣṇa escapes Kaṃsa's hands and takes to the hills, and attaching her to the great goddess. When the sahasranāma gives Lalitā the name, the absorption is complete and no longer needs explaining.

Viṣṇumāyā is the fourth name in this batch that hands her another deity's property. The Devī Māhātmya has a long litany in which the goddess is saluted under the name of whatever she is in all beings, and viṣṇumāyā heads the list. Behind the name is the story from that text's first chapter, in which the sleep that holds Viṣṇu is a goddess, and she must withdraw before he can wake and act. Read that way the compound is not saying she belongs to Viṣṇu; it is saying that the power everyone calls Viṣṇu's is a person, that she has her own name, and that Viṣṇu is at her disposal rather than the other way round.

Vilāsinī closes the verse with the tradition's favourite word for what the world is. The dictionary's sense for the noun is a lively, charming, coquettish woman, but vilāsa in this literature is a technical term: the shining-out or sporting of consciousness, manifestation undertaken for no reason except that it is in her nature to manifest. It is the word in the title of the Kāmakalāvilāsa, the treatise behind the second name of verse 73, where it names the unfolding of the point into a world. Placed at the end of a verse that has just called her greater than the universe, the ordainer, and the māyā of Viṣṇu, it defuses all three. What looks from below like arrangement, illusion and immensity is, from her side, play.
commentary.practice:
Seven names, all beginning with v, and the caesura falls after vedavedyā and after vedajananī. That leaves the two longest names, vindhyācalanivāsinī and the pair viṣṇumāyā vilāsinī, filling the second half of each line.

The great gift of this verse is that it puts all three Sanskrit sibilants in it, and the contrast is easy to hear once pointed out. Viśvādhikā has ś, the palatal, made with the tongue against the hard palate — the nearest English sound is the sh of "sheep", said with the tongue flat and forward. Viṣṇumāyā has ṣ, the retroflex, made with the tongue-tip curled well back, a duller and darker sound. Vilāsinī has plain dental s, the tip at the teeth. Say viśva, viṣṇu, vilāsinī in a row, three times, and this verse will have taught you the distinction that the whole stotra depends on.

Vindhyācalanivāsinī opens with a three-consonant cluster, न्ध्य: n, then the aspirated dh, then y. All three are dental or palatal and close together, so the sequence is fast rather than difficult, but the aspiration must be audible — vindhya, not vindya. The same aspirated dh returns immediately in vidhātrī, where it is followed by the cluster tr, so the second line begins with two clusters in five syllables: vi-dhā-trī.

Viśvādhikā contains a sandhi worth reconstructing: viśva plus adhikā, two short a sounds merged into one long ā, giving viśvādhikā and hiding the word-boundary completely. This is the commonest vowel sandhi in the language and the one that most often defeats a beginner trying to look a name up in a dictionary. Split it before you search.

Viṣṇumāyā has the cluster ṣṇ, retroflex sibilant into retroflex nasal — the tongue curls back for the ṣ and stays exactly where it is for the ṇ, with no movement between them. This is the same economy you met in aṣṭamī in verse 5 and will meet again in the ṣ names of verse 84. Keep the u short: viṣ-ṇu, not viṣ-ṇū.

Watch the ordinary vowels too. Vedavedyā has four short e and a sounds and one long ā, and the dy in the middle is dental d into y. Vedajananī is five short vowels and a long ī at the end, the lightest name in the verse; vidhātrī, immediately before it, is two longs and nothing else. Alternating those two correctly is what gives the second line its shape.

On what to hold while chanting: the verse is an exercise in refusing to choose between the vast and the local. It is easy to chant the abstractions with attention and let the mountain go past as a piece of geography, and that is the wrong way round. The tradition's claim is not that she is everywhere in general. It is that she is everywhere and also in the Vindhyas in particular, where there is a temple with a queue outside it, and that neither statement weakens the other. Ten verses further on the hymn will name two more places by name, and this is where it starts.

076.subtitle: The field, the knower of the field, and the one who guards both

commentary.meaning: Five names, every one of them opening with the conjunct kṣ, and four of the five built on a single word: kṣetra, a field. The verse takes a technical term from the thirteenth chapter of the Bhagavad Gītā and works it in three positions. She is the field — the body and the whole spread of nature that is worked on. She is the mistress of the field. And then, in the longest name, she is the guardian of both the field and the one who knows it, which is a different claim from either of the first two, because it makes her neither term in the classical pair but the thing that keeps the pair in being. The fourth name steps outside the analysis: free of waning and waxing, exempt from the increase and decrease that everything on a field is subject to. Then the last name drops back to earth and to the other meaning of the word. A kṣetra is also a piece of consecrated ground, and the kṣetrapālas who stand guard at its edge are among her worshippers.
commentary.history:
The Gītā's thirteenth chapter opens by defining its terms: this body is called the field, and the one who knows it is called the knower of the field. The pair is inherited from Sāṃkhya, where the whole of nature stands over against a consciousness that is not part of it, and it is the most economical apparatus classical Indian thought has for stating the difference between what is observed and what observes. Kṛṣṇa then makes his own move: know me also as the knower of the field in every field. The stotra is quoting the same chapter, and the first two names track it faithfully — she is the field, and she is the field's ruler.

The third name does something else. Kṣetrakṣetrajñapālinī makes her the protector of the field and of the knower, which puts her outside the pair rather than on either side of it. Where the Gītā identifies the god with the knowing term, this verse declines to. The reason is not obscure once the rest of the hymn is in view: within the same fifteen verses she will be called pure consciousness, the referent of the word "that", and, at name 385, the one who has no witness. A tradition that will eventually say the witness itself needs no second witness cannot rest with making her the witness of the field. So she guards the pair, and the pair is not the last thing there is.

Kṣayavṛddhivinirmuktā is the pivot. Kṣaya and vṛddhi are the standard terms for the moon's waning and waxing; they are also the words for loss and gain in an account, and for the decay and growth of a body. What has a field undergoes both. The name says she does not — which is the plain sense of pūrṇa, full, in the famous verse in which fullness taken from fullness leaves fullness behind. Read against the neighbouring verses this is more pointed than it looks: two verses back she was called kalāvatī, possessor of the digits, and nine verses on she will be the sixteen eternal goddesses. The digits of the moon are exactly the things that wax and wane. The tradition's answer is the sixteenth digit, the one that is said to remain when the other fifteen have gone; and a name declaring her free of waxing and waning is a way of saying which digit she is.

The last name changes register completely, and the pun that lets it do so is old. Kṣetra is a field of grain, a field of enquiry, the body, and a holy place — Kurukṣetra is a kṣetra in the last sense, and so is any temple town. A kṣetrapāla is, in the dictionary's flat first gloss, a man employed to guard fields; in practice it is the tutelary deity of a sacred site, usually a form of Bhairava, whose shrine stands at the boundary rather than in the sanctum and who receives offerings the principal deity would not accept. These are frequently the older, more local, less brahminical powers of the place, given a post at the gate when the temple was built over them. Monier-Williams notes drily that their number is given as forty-nine. Saying that the kṣetrapālas worship her is therefore a statement about religious politics as much as about theology: the fierce guardians at the edge of the ground are inside her hierarchy.

And the two senses of kṣetra are not kept apart. The body is a field, a temple is a field, and the tantric traditions built a whole system on the identity — mapping named sacred places onto sites in the practitioner's own body, so that going on pilgrimage and sitting still could be described in the same vocabulary. Six and seven verses further on this hymn will name Jālandhara and Oḍyāṇa, two of the four great seats, and expect the reader to hear both a map and an anatomy. This verse, with its five kṣ names, is where the equipment for that is assembled.
commentary.practice:
The conjunct is the whole verse. क्ष is not a single sound and is not the x of English "axe": it is k released directly into the retroflex sibilant ṣ. Say a clean unaspirated k, then curl the tongue-tip back for the ṣ, and join them without a vowel between. Regional habits vary a good deal — some reciters produce something close to kkh, others to ksh with a palatal — and the analytic k plus ṣ is what the letters say. You get five consecutive chances to build the habit here, which is why this verse is one of the best drills in the hymn.

After kṣ comes tra in three of the names: a dental t, tongue-tip at the teeth, and then the tapped r. Kṣetra is two syllables, kṣe-tra, and the e is long — every e and o in Sanskrit is long, which is why kṣetra scans heavy and why the metre works. Kṣetrakṣetrajñapālinī then puts the whole cluster in twice and finishes with jña, so the name runs kṣe-tra-kṣe-tra-jña-pā-li-nī and fills a half-line exactly. Practise it as two halves joined: kṣetra-kṣetrajña, then pālinī.

Kṣayavṛddhivinirmuktā contains the syllabic ṛ, which is a vowel and must be short — one beat, with the tongue in roughly the retroflex position. Northern reciters generally approximate it with ri and southern reciters with ru; whichever you use, do not let it stretch. Then comes ddh, a doubled consonant of which only the second half is aspirated: hold the d closed for a full beat and release the breath once, at the end. Vṛddhi with a short ṛ, a long held d, and one puff.

The fifth name is easier than it looks: kṣetra-pāla-sama-arcitā, with sam and arcitā fusing into samarcitā. The c of arcitā is the unaspirated palatal, the ch of "church" without the puff of air; and the r before it is a tap, not a colouring of the vowel.

The caesura is clean at eight in both lines, and the second half of the first line is a single eight-syllable name. Reciters often accelerate slightly across kṣetrakṣetrajñapālinī because the repetition invites it. Resist that: the two occurrences of kṣetra are the whole point of the name, and blurring them loses the pair the name is protecting.

One thing to hold in mind while chanting. This is the most purely philosophical verse so far in the hymn, and it is worth noticing that it does not sound philosophical. It sounds like five hammer-blows on the same consonant. The technical content — a Sāṃkhya distinction, a Vedāntic refusal, a lunar doctrine, and a note about village guardian shrines — arrives inside a piece of deliberate sound-patterning that a child could recognise as a set. That combination is characteristic of the whole text, and this verse is the clearest place to notice it.

077.subtitle: Tender to whoever bows, and seated in the ring of fire

commentary.meaning: Seven names on v, and the verse falls into two unequal halves. The first four are moral: she is victory, she is stainless, she is the one before whom bowing is right — and then, in the longest of the four, she is vatsalā towards those who do bow, which is the word for what a cow feels for her calf. That fourth name quietly converts the third from a statement about her worth into a statement about a relationship. The second line leaves ethics behind. She is the speaker of the word wherever speech occurs; her hair is beautiful; and her seat is the circle of fire. The verse ends by putting her somewhere, as the verse two before it did, but the place this time is not on any map. It is a region of the practitioner's own body, and the reader is expected to know that.
commentary.history:
Vijayā is a name in its own right before it is an adjective. Durgā's two companions in purāṇic iconography are Jayā and Vijayā, and this hymn distributes them: vijayā here at name 346, jayā at 377 six verses later. Vijayā is also one of the sixteen Nityās, the goddesses of the lunar days whose company the hymn will make her body at name 391. Names in this text are rarely only descriptions; a good proportion of them are also somebody, and the reader who knows the pantheon hears a second layer that the translation cannot carry.

Vandārujanavatsalā repays being taken apart. Vandāru is a rare word — the dictionary gives praising, reverential, polite — and jana is simply people, so vandārujana is the reverent sort of person. Vatsala is the specific one. It comes from vatsa, a calf, and the dictionary's first sense is affectionate towards offspring, with the illustration being a cow longing for her calf. Vātsalya became one of the standard categories of devotional feeling in later bhakti literature, always with the animal image intact. So the name is not saying she is kind in general. It is saying that towards people who bow she has the particular helpless attachment of a cow to a calf, and that the tenderness is a response — it is directed at vandāru-jana, the ones who bow, and the previous name has just said that bowing is the appropriate thing to do.

Vāgvādinī brings speech into the verse, four verses before the hymn devotes an entire verse to the stages of speech. The name has a further resonance in this particular text. The Lalitopākhyāna says that the thousand names were composed by the Vāgdevatās — the goddesses of speech, Vaśinī and her seven companions — at Lalitā's own command, and that they recited them in her presence. A name meaning "she who speaks the word" is therefore close to a statement about how the hymn thinks it exists: the goddesses of speech spoke it, and she is the one speaking wherever speech occurs.

Vāmakeśī reads as an ordinary compliment — vāma is lovely, dear, beautiful, and keśa is hair — and it may be no more than that. But vāma also means left, and Vāmakeśvara is the title of the root tantra of this tradition. The Vāmakeśvarīmata, whose first section is called the Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava, the ocean of the sixteen Nityās, and whose companion text is the Yoginīhṛdaya, is the closest thing Śrīvidyā has to a foundational scripture, and Jayaratha's commentary on it is among the tradition's central works. Eight verses further on the hymn will call her nityāṣoḍaśikārūpā. Between them, vāmakeśī here and that name there put both halves of the title of the tradition's root text into the thousand names. The ambiguity of vāma — lovely and left, the beautiful and the left-hand path — is one the tradition has lived with for a thousand years, and nothing in the name resolves it.

Vahnimaṇḍalavāsinī places her in the fire. Tantric physiology divides the body into three regions, the circles of fire, sun and moon, running from the base of the trunk to the crown, and the same three are mapped onto the Śrīcakra and onto the divisions of the mantra. The fire circle is the lowest and hottest, and it is where the coiled power sleeps. Śaṅkara's ninth verse walks up through the whole scheme, placing earth, water, fire, air and space in successive centres and ending at the thousand-petalled lotus. There is also a letter-level connection that is hard to ignore in this stretch of the text: the seed syllable of fire is raṃ, and Monier-Williams records vahni as a mystical name of the letter r — six verses after the run of sixteen names beginning with that letter. Whether or not the composers arranged it, the material is all of a piece.
commentary.practice:
The v's are relentless and the verse will expose whatever your habit with them is. A Sanskrit v is a light approach of the lower lip to the upper teeth, without the strong buzz of an English v and without the full lip-rounding of an English w; the sound sits between the two. Crucially it is not a b. If vandyā and bandhyā sound alike in your mouth, this verse is the one to fix it on.

The first line stacks three consonant clusters in eight syllables: the ndy of vandyā, then the nd of vandāru, then the ts of vatsalā. Vandyā is van-dyā, with the dental d joined to y; do not insert a vowel. Vatsalā has t followed by the dental sibilant s, a sequence English only has across word boundaries — think of the end of "cats" and then attach a lā to it.

Vāgvādinī shows a voicing sandhi in the script. The word is vāc, speech, plus vādinī, and a final c before a voiced sound becomes g: वाग्वादिनी. So the k-series letter you see is the trace of a c you cannot hear, and the same change is at work in vāgdevatā, the name for the goddesses who are said to have composed this hymn. Say vāg-vā-di-nī with the g fully voiced and the two v's distinct.

Vahnimaṇḍalavāsinī is the long one and has three separate difficulties. First the hn of vahni, written ह्न, a voiced h running into n — the same class of problem as the hv of vihvalā three verses back, and solved the same way, by keeping the voice on through the h rather than treating it as a breath. Then the ṇḍ of maṇḍala, both retroflex, tongue curled back and staying back. Then the plain dental s of vāsinī, which after all those retroflexes wants to curl back too and must not.

The caesura is at eight in both lines and both second halves are single names, so the rhythm of the verse is three short names, one long, two short names, one long. Take the breath after vandyā if you need one, not in the middle of the fourth name.

A note on the ā's. Vijayā and vimalā are light, three short syllables and a long; vandyā is heavy from the first syllable because of the cluster; vāgvādinī, vāmakeśī and vahni- all begin with a long ā except the last. Getting vahni- short at the start of an eight-syllable name, after two names that started long, is the small technical demand of the second line.

For contemplation, the last name gives an instruction rather than an image. It says where to put the attention: low, at the base, in the region the tradition calls fire. It is worth noticing that the hymn has arranged the sequence so that this comes immediately after four names about conduct and reverence and one about speech. The move from the ethical to the physiological happens without a seam, and the text plainly does not regard them as different subjects.

crossReferences.translation: Earth at the root-support, water at the jewelled city, the carrier of oblations at your own place, air at the heart, space above that, and mind between the brows — piercing every one of them, the whole way of the kula, you sport in secret with your husband in the thousand-petalled lotus.
crossReferences.relevance: The circle of fire in this verse is one station of the ascent Śaṅkara sets out here — hutavaha, the carrier of oblations, is fire, and he assigns it to svādhiṣṭhāna. Placements differ between texts and lineages, which is worth knowing before treating any single scheme as the scheme. What does not vary is the structure: fire low, moon at the crown, and a route between them that the practitioner is said to travel.
